title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: Anatole Kuragin was staying in Moscow because his father had sent him away from Petersburg, where he had been spending twenty thousand rubles a year in cash, besides running up debts for just as much more, which his creditors demanded from his father.

His father informed him that he would pay half his debts for the last time, but only on condition that he went to Moscow as adjutant to the commander in chief — a post his father had obtained for him — and would at last try to make a good match there. He pointed him toward Princess Mary and Julie Karagina.

Anatole agreed and went to Moscow, where he moved in with Pierre. Pierre received him unwillingly at first, but got used to him after a while, sometimes even went with him on his wild nights out, and gave him money in the form of loans.

As Shinshin had noted, since his arrival Anatole had turned the heads of the Moscow ladies, especially because he ignored them and plainly preferred gypsy girls and French actresses — with the chief of whom, Mademoiselle George, he was said to be intimate. He had never missed a wild party at Danilov's or at the gatherings of other Moscow revelers, drank whole nights through, outdoing everyone else, and was at all the balls and parties of the best society. There was talk of his affairs with some of the ladies, and he flirted with a few of them at balls. But he didn't chase the unmarried girls, especially the rich heiresses who were mostly plain. There was a special reason for this, as he had gotten married two years before — a fact known only to his closest friends. While stationed with his regiment in Poland, a Polish landowner of modest means had forced him to marry his daughter. Anatole had very soon abandoned his wife and, in exchange for payments he agreed to send to his father-in-law, had arranged to pass himself off as a bachelor.

Anatole was always content with his situation, with himself, and with others. He was instinctively and thoroughly convinced that it was impossible for him to live otherwise than as he did, and that he had never in his life done anything wrong. He was incapable of considering how his actions might affect others or what the consequences might be. He was convinced that, just as a duck is made to live in water, God had made him such that he must spend thirty thousand rubles a year and always occupy a prominent position in society. He believed this so firmly that others, looking at him, were persuaded of it too and didn't refuse him either a leading place in society or money, which he borrowed from anyone and everyone and clearly would never repay.

He was not a gambler — at any rate he didn't care about winning. He was not vain. He didn't care what people thought of him. Still less could he be accused of ambition. More than once he had annoyed his father by ruining his own career, and he laughed at honors of all kinds. He wasn't stingy, and didn't refuse anyone who asked him. All he cared about was fun and women, and since in his view there was nothing dishonorable in these pursuits, and he was incapable of considering what indulging them cost others, he honestly considered himself blameless, sincerely despised rogues and bad people, and with a clear conscience carried his head high.

Rakes — those male Magdalenes — have a secret feeling of innocence similar to that of female Magdalenes, based on the same hope of forgiveness. "All will be forgiven her, for she loved much; and all will be forgiven him, for he enjoyed much."

Dolokhov, who had reappeared that year in Moscow after his exile and his Persian adventures, and was leading a life of luxury, gambling, and excess, reconnected with his old Petersburg comrade Kuragin and made use of him for his own ends.

Anatole was genuinely fond of Dolokhov for his cleverness and daring. Dolokhov, who needed Anatole Kuragin's name, position, and connections as bait to lure rich young men into his gambling circle, used him and amused himself at his expense without letting the other realize it. Apart from the advantage he gained from Anatole, the very process of dominating another's will was in itself a pleasure, a habit, and a necessity for Dolokhov.

Natasha had made a strong impression on Kuragin. At supper after the opera he described to Dolokhov with the air of a connoisseur the appeal of her arms, shoulders, feet, and hair, and declared his intention of pursuing her. Anatole had no idea and was incapable of imagining what might come of such a pursuit, as he never considered the outcome of any of his actions.
"She's first-rate, my dear fellow, but not for us," replied Dolokhov.
"I'll tell my sister to invite her to dinner," said Anatole. "Eh?"
"You know, I adore young girls — they lose their heads at once," Anatole went on.
"You've been caught once already by a 'young girl,'" said Dolokhov, who knew about Kuragin's marriage. "Watch out!"
"Well, that can't happen twice! Eh?" said Anatole, with a good-natured laugh.
